text: A class that owns a raw resource must write all five (the rule of five ), because the compiler-written copy would copy the pointer, not the buffer: rule_of_five.cpp (lines 5 to 29) // A class that owns a raw buffer must write all five special members. class Buffer { float * data_; std::size_t n_; public : explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_( new float [n]()), n_(n) {} ~Buffer() { delete [] data_; } // 1 destructor Buffer( const Buffer& o) : data_( new float [o.n_]), n_(o.n_) { // 2 copy constructor std::memcpy(data_, o.data_, n_ * sizeof ( float )); } Buffer& operator =( const Buffer& o) { // 3 copy assignment Buffer tmp(o); swap(tmp); return * this ; } Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept // 4 move constructor : data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr )), n_(std::exchange(o.n_, 0)) {} Buffer& operator =(Buffer&& o) noexcept { // 5 move assignment Buffer tmp(std::move(o)); swap(tmp); return * this ; } void swap(Buffer& o) noexcept { std::swap(data_, o.data_); std::swap(n_, o.n_); } std::size_t size() const { return n_; } }; rule_of_five.cpp (lines 31 to 35) // Rule of zero: let a member that already manages itself do the work. #include <vector> struct Buffer0 { std::vector< float > data; // the compiler writes all five, correctly }; $ clang++ -std=c++23 -O2 -Wall -Wextra rule_of_five.cpp -o rule_of_five && ./rule_of_five b 4, c 4, moved-from a 0; y 4, z 4, moved-from x 0 Thirty lines of careful code against one line ( std::vector<float> data; ), with the same behaviour: copies get their own buffer, moved-from objects are empty.
